  cautiously, about one segment per round trip. This is the "additive increase"
  part of the classic AIMD rule (additive increase, multiplicative decrease).
  The sender keeps probing for extra bandwidth, but gently.

  Loss is the main signal that the network is congested. If three duplicate
  acknowledgments arrive, the sender assumes a single packet was dropped while
  later ones got through. It performs fast retransmit, resends the missing
  segment, and cuts the window roughly in half (the multiplicative decrease). It
  then continues in fast recovery without restarting from scratch. If a timeout
  occurs instead, the situation looks more serious. The window collapses to one
  segment (or the initial window) and slow start begins again, with ssthresh
  set to half the previous window.

  The result is the familiar sawtooth pattern: the window rises steadily, drops
  sharply when loss occurs, then rises again. AIMD also helps competing flows
  converge toward a fair share of a bottleneck link.

  Modern variants refine this. CUBIC, the default on Linux, grows the window
  along a cubic curve, which suits high-bandwidth, high-latency paths. BBR does
